title: How a compiler works

source.title: Stiti demo lesson (own examples, not from a book)

cues.say: Hey! Today we'll figure out what a compiler actually does when you hit compile.

ops.text: Goal: the phases of a compiler

cues.say: Chalo, before I explain anything, take a quick guess.

check.prompt: Guess: when you run gcc main.c, what is the very FIRST thing the compiler does with your file?
expectations: reads the characters and groups them into tokens or words
check.reveal: Hold that thought. We'll come back to your guess at the end.

cues.say: In one line: a compiler translates your source code into target code, without changing what it means.
Think of it like a translator who reads Hindi, understands it, and then writes English.
So inside there are two big halves. The front end understands, and the back end generates.
Three words we'll use: token, syntax tree, and intermediate code.
Let's take one real line of code: position equals initial plus rate times sixty.
Phase one is the lexer. It reads characters and chops them into tokens, like words in a sentence.
Phase two is the parser. It checks the grammar and builds a syntax tree from those tokens.
Phase three is semantic analysis. It checks meaning, like whether the types actually fit together.
Here, if rate is a float and sixty is an int, it quietly turns sixty into sixty point zero.

check.prompt: Someone writes: int x = ;  The value after = is missing. Which phase catches this error?
expectations: the parser, because every token is valid but the grammar rule is broken
hints: Every token there is a valid word: int, x, equals, semicolon.
So the words are fine. Which phase checks the grammar rules?
check.reveal: It's the parser. Each token is valid, but the grammar says an expression must come after equals. Grammar errors are the parser's job.
check.on_correct: Exactly. The words were fine, the grammar was broken, so the parser catches it.

cues.say: This is the tree the parser builds for our line.
Notice the multiply sits lowest, so it gets evaluated first. That's operator precedence, built into the shape.
And the root is the assignment, because storing into position happens last.
Now the back end. First, the tree becomes simple intermediate code, one small step per line.

ops.text: Back end: making the machine code

cues.say: Then the optimizer makes it faster, for example by doing the int to float conversion once, at compile time.
Finally the code generator picks real registers and real machine instructions.
One more thing. A symbol table runs alongside every phase, remembering each name and its type.

ops.text: Symbol table: position, initial, rate → float

check.prompt: Why don't compilers jump straight from the syntax tree to machine code? Why have intermediate code in the middle?
expectations: one intermediate code lets the same front end work with many different machines or back ends
optimization is easier on simple intermediate code
hints: Imagine three languages and four different CPUs. How many full compilers would you need without a shared middle?
Also, is it easier to improve a big tree or a list of tiny simple steps?
check.reveal: Two reasons. One shared intermediate code means any front end can plug into any back end, so you don't rebuild everything per machine. And simple step-by-step code is much easier to optimize.
check.on_correct: Nice reasoning. Reuse across machines, and easier optimization.

cues.say: Quick quiz, no peeking. I'll hide the board for a moment.

check.prompt: Name the three front end phases, in order.
hints: The first one chops characters into tokens.
check.reveal: Lexer, then parser, then semantic analysis. Tokens, tree, meaning.

cues.say: Last one.

check.prompt: Your program uses a variable called total that was never declared. Which phase reports that?
expectations: semantic analysis, because the grammar is fine but the name has no declaration
hints: total is a perfectly valid token, and the line follows the grammar.
So which phase checks meaning, using the symbol table?
check.reveal: Semantic analysis. The grammar is fine, but the symbol table has no entry for total, so the meaning check fails.
check.on_correct: Yes! Grammar fine, meaning broken. Semantic check.

cues.say: Let's wrap up with the three big ideas.
The front end understands your code: tokens, then a tree, then a meaning check.
The middle is simple intermediate code that the optimizer can improve.
And the back end turns it into real machine instructions. I've saved five revision cards for tomorrow.

summary: Intermediate code makes optimization and reuse easy
Back end: registers and machine instructions

cards.back: Tokens (like words), e.g. id = id + id * num
The parser: tokens are valid, the grammar is broken

cards.front: Which phase catches an undeclared variable?
Why is * lower than + in the syntax tree?
cards.back: Lower nodes are evaluated first: precedence is built into the tree shape
Any front end can reuse any back end, and simple code is easier to optimize
